jurisdiction.name: LGPD
jurisdiction.fullName: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais

articles.surfaceLabel: Does Brazil's Privacy Law Apply to Your Organization?
articles.plainSummary: Brazil's privacy law applies to any organization that processes personal information about people in Brazil, regardless of where the organization is located. It also applies if the processing happens in Brazil or if the data was collected in Brazil.
articles.personalImpact: Massive leaks have exposed the CPF numbers and records of millions of Brazilians. That data fuels fraud, spam, and unfair profiling. This law sets binding rules for almost any organization handling data of people in Brazil.
articles.professionalLayer: The LGPD applies to any natural or legal person, public or private, that carries out processing operations of personal data of individuals located in Brazil, regardless of the nationality or country of headquarters of the organization. Territorial scope also covers processing that takes place in Brazil or processing of data collected in Brazil. The LGPD is broadly GDPR-aligned in structure. It establishes 10 legal bases for processing, a set of data subject rights, requirements for a data protection officer called the Encarregado, impact reports when the ANPD asks for them, breach notification, and international transfer mechanisms. Key structural differences from GDPR include a broader set of legal bases and a different treatment of legitimate interests. A February 2026 law made the ANPD a national regulatory agency, the Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados. In August 2026 it issued its first large fine, R$153.7 million against ByteDance, TikTok's owner, over children's data. The deadline for an appeal to the ANPD board has passed. Brazil's standard contractual clauses took effect in August 2024, and contracts had to adopt them by August 2025. In January 2026, Brazil and the EU recognized each other as giving adequate protection.
articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization process personal data of individuals located in Brazil, process data in Brazil, or collect data in Brazil, and have you mapped which of the LGPD's 10 legal bases applies to each processing activity?

gapRemediation.smb: Assess whether the LGPD applies based on the territorial scope criteria. If it does, the 10 legal bases framework means you cannot rely on the same legal basis structure as the GDPR without reviewing each processing activity against the LGPD's specific requirements.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Organizations already compliant with the GDPR have a strong structural foundation for the LGPD but should not assume equivalence. Legal bases, consent standards, DPO requirements, and transfer mechanisms all have LGPD-specific requirements.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise LGPD programs require a gap assessment against GDPR compliance to identify LGPD-specific obligations. ANPD regulatory guidance is evolving. Your program should include an ANPD monitoring process similar to EDPB monitoring for the GDPR.

articles.surfaceLabel: Why a Company Is Allowed to Use Your Information in Brazil
articles.plainSummary: Like the GDPR, Brazil's privacy law requires companies to have a valid legal reason to process your personal information. Brazil's law provides 10 possible reasons, more than the GDPR's six, including some that are unique to Brazil's legal and social context.
articles.personalImpact: A company holding your data cannot simply use it however it likes. Every use is meant to rest on a specific, lawful reason. Article 7 sets out the limited grounds, such as your consent or a contract.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 7 establishes 10 lawful bases for processing personal data under the LGPD. They are consent, compliance with a legal or regulatory obligation, execution of public policies, research by a research body, and execution of a contract or pre-contractual procedures. They also include the exercise of rights in judicial, administrative, or arbitration proceedings, protection of life or physical safety, health protection by health professionals or entities, legitimate interests of the controller or third parties, and credit protection. Legitimate interests need a balancing test, and Article 10 adds purpose, necessity, and transparency conditions. The ANPD set out its approach in a February 2024 guide. Legitimate interests cannot justify processing sensitive data. Credit protection is a standalone basis, reflecting Brazil's credit bureau ecosystem.
articles.assessTrigger: Has your organization mapped a specific LGPD legal basis to each processing activity, and where you rely on legitimate interests, have you documented that assessment against the ANPD's 2024 guide?

gapRemediation.smb: Review each processing activity against the LGPD's 10 bases. Consent-based processing requires the same quality of consent as the GDPR. The credit protection basis is relevant for any organization involved in credit assessment or financial services.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Your RoPA equivalent under LGPD should document the legal basis for each processing activity. Where you have mapped GDPR legal bases, a parallel LGPD mapping exercise is required. The bases do not map one-to-one.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise legal basis mapping for LGPD should be integrated with your global privacy program. Legitimate interest assessments should follow the balancing test in the ANPD's 2024 guide.

comparisonFlags.note: The LGPD has 10 legal bases. The GDPR has six. Additional bases include credit protection, health by professionals, and public policy.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Know If and What Data Is Held about You
articles.plainSummary: You have the right to ask any organization whether it holds personal information about you and, if it does, to receive a copy of that information. This right applies to any organization operating under Brazil's privacy law.
articles.personalImpact: Your score with a credit bureau like Serasa can decide a loan, a rental, or a plan. Yet the data behind it often stays out of sight. Article 18 lets you ask what a company holds on you and receive a copy.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 18 grants data subjects in Brazil a set of rights that closely parallel GDPR Chapter III rights. Article 18, items I and II, give the right to confirm processing and access data. This mirrors Article 15 of the GDPR. Responses must be provided in simplified or complete form as requested by the data subject. The format requirement, simplified versus complete, is an LGPD-specific nuance without direct GDPR equivalent. A simplified reply is due immediately. A complete reply is due within 15 days of the request, compared to the GDPR's one-month standard. Small businesses get 15 days for a simplified reply and 30 days for a complete one, unless their processing is high-risk. Public bodies follow their own deadlines.
articles.responseTimeline: Simplified reply: immediately. Complete reply: within 15 days of the request. Small businesses: 15 days for a simplified reply and 30 days for a complete one, unless their processing is high-risk.
articles.assessTrigger: Can your organization reply to access requests immediately in simplified form, and within 15 days in complete form, as the data subject chooses?

gapRemediation.smb: A response template covering both simplified and complete formats is the starting point. The 15-day window for a complete reply is shorter than the GDPR. Small businesses get 30 days unless their processing is high-risk. Ensure your intake and fulfillment process can meet it.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Your DSR process should be tested against the LGPD's immediate and 15-day deadlines specifically. Organizations that built processes for the GDPR's one-month window may not meet the LGPD's shorter requirement.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise DSR platforms should be configured for the LGPD's immediate and 15-day deadlines separately from the GDPR's one-month SLA. Simplified versus complete format preference should be captured at intake.

comparisonFlags.note: The LGPD requires a complete access reply within 15 days. The GDPR allows one month extendable to three. The LGPD is more demanding on response speed.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Remove or Restrict Your Data
articles.plainSummary: You have the right to ask organizations to make your personal information anonymous, to block it from being used, or to delete it, particularly where it was processed without a valid legal basis.
articles.personalImpact: Every company that keeps your data is one more place a leak can strike. Old records you forgot about still sit on their servers. Article 18 lets you ask for data that is no longer needed to be deleted.
articles.professionalLayer: Where data is unnecessary, excessive, or processed in violation of the LGPD, Article 18, item IV, lets the person ask for anonymization, blocking, or deletion. This is similar to the GDPR's right to erasure but differs in scope. Article 18, VI separately lets data subjects ask for deletion of data processed on consent, with limited exceptions. Anonymization as a consumer remedy is an LGPD-specific option. Blocking, which suspends processing, parallels the GDPR's restriction of processing under Article 18. The availability of anonymization as a consumer-facing remedy creates operational complexity since true anonymization is technically demanding and irreversible. Controllers must immediately tell anyone they shared the data with, so they can repeat the correction or deletion.
articles.responseTimeline: Act immediately, or reply explaining why action is not immediate. The law leaves a fixed deadline to a future ANPD regulation.
articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization have processes for all three remedies: anonymization, blocking, and deletion, and do you have a technical definition of anonymization that meets the LGPD's standard?

gapRemediation.smb: Define what anonymization means technically for your organization. Blocking and deletion processes aligned with your DSR workflow are the practical starting point.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Your DSR process should include defined responses for each of the three remedies. Technical anonymization capability requires assessment. True anonymization must be irreversible.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise programs need documented technical standards for anonymization that are defensible to ANPD. Blocking workflows should integrate with your active processing systems.

comparisonFlags.note: LGPD explicitly offers anonymization as a data subject remedy. GDPR focuses on erasure and restriction. Anonymization appears as a data protection technique rather than a consumer right.

articles.surfaceLabel: What Happens When Personal Data Is Compromised in Brazil
articles.plainSummary: Organizations in Brazil must notify the national data protection authority and affected individuals when a security incident could cause harm to data subjects.
articles.personalImpact: Given Brazil's history of large-scale leaks, a breach of your data is a real risk. The danger grows when a company stays silent about it. Article 48 requires notice to the ANPD and to you when the risk is serious.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 48 requires controllers to notify the ANPD and affected data subjects of security incidents that could cause relevant harm to data subjects. The LGPD does not specify a fixed notification timeframe in the legislation. ANPD Resolution CD/ANPD No. 15/2024 requires notification to the ANPD and affected data subjects within three business days of becoming aware of the incident, with supplementary information within 20 business days. Small processing agents, including startups and small businesses under ANPD Resolution CD/ANPD No. 2/2022, receive double the deadlines, six business days and 40 for the supplement, unless they carry out high-risk processing. The doubling does not apply where the incident could endanger people's physical or moral integrity. This is a materially different timeline from the GDPR's 72-hour window.
articles.responseTimeline: Notification to the ANPD and affected data subjects: three business days from awareness. Supplementary information within 20 business days.
articles.assessTrigger: Does your organization's breach response plan address the LGPD's specific notification timelines, and is your ANPD notification process documented separately from your GDPR supervisory authority notification process?

gapRemediation.smb: A documented breach response checklist covering the LGPD's 3-business-day notification window is a reasonable starting point. Startups and small businesses get six business days, unless their processing is high-risk. Do not assume your GDPR process covers the LGPD.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Your breach response plan should include jurisdiction-specific notification timelines. The LGPD's 3-business-day notification is tighter than it appears in practice.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise breach response programs should have separate notification workflows for each jurisdiction. The LGPD's two-stage notification process requires distinct internal processes for preliminary and supplementary filings.

comparisonFlags.note: The LGPD uses two stages: notice within three business days, then more detail within 20 business days. The GDPR has a single 72-hour window.

articles.plainSummary: Transferring personal information from Brazil to other countries is only permitted under specific conditions designed to ensure the data remains protected at an equivalent level.
articles.personalImpact: Your data often moves to servers in other countries with different rules. Without safeguards, its protection could weaken on arrival. Articles 33 to 36 require LGPD-level protection to remain in place abroad.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 33 permits international transfers on nine grounds. They include countries the ANPD recognizes as adequate, specific or standard contractual clauses, global corporate rules, and certifications. Others cover legal cooperation, protection of life, ANPD authorization, public policy, and specific consent. The ANPD's standard contractual clauses took effect in August 2024, and contracts had to adopt them by August 2025. Its first adequacy decision, in January 2026, recognizes the EU and EEA. The EU recognized Brazil the same day, so EU-Brazil transfers no longer need clauses. For other countries, organizations relying on standard clauses should use the ANPD's version. GDPR SCCs have no automatic recognition under the LGPD.
articles.assessTrigger: Has your organization identified all international data transfers involving Brazilian personal data, and are you using ANPD-approved transfer mechanisms rather than assuming GDPR SCCs are sufficient?

gapRemediation.smb: Identify every country your Brazilian user data flows to. Confirm each transfer relies on a valid LGPD mechanism. Transfers to the EU and EEA are covered by adequacy. GDPR SCCs are not automatically valid under the LGPD.
gapRemediation.midMarket: A transfer mapping exercise for Brazilian data flows should be conducted separately from your GDPR mapping. ANPD-approved SCCs should be implemented for transfers that rely on contractual clauses.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Enterprise LGPD transfer programs require systematic mapping, ANPD SCC implementation, and monitoring of new ANPD adequacy decisions beyond the EU and EEA.

comparisonFlags.note: Clause-based LGPD transfers must use ANPD standard clauses or approved specific clauses. GDPR SCCs have no automatic recognition under the LGPD. EU-Brazil transfers rely on mutual adequacy since January 2026.
